paragraphs.text: I used to be proud of doing five things at once, but I have come to believe multitasking is mostly a myth rather than a real skill.

Contrary to popular belief, the human brain does not perform two demanding tasks simultaneously; instead, it engages in rapid task-switching, reallocating attention from one activity to another in quick succession.
Each of these switches carries a measurable cognitive cost, often referred to as a switch cost, which degrades both the speed and the accuracy with which the subsequent task is completed.
When I tried to text my friend while writing a lab report last semester, both came out worse, and it took longer than if I had just done them one at a time.
Supporters say constant multitasking trains your brain to juggle, but the evidence points the other way.

Studies of heavy media multitaskers have found that frequent switchers tend to perform more poorly on tests of attention filtering and working memory, suggesting that the habit erodes rather than strengthens the capacity for sustained focus.
It may help to think of attention as a single spotlight that can only illuminate one area at a time, rather than a floodlight covering everything at once.
So instead of cultivating multitasking, I think students are better off cultivating focus, since deep single-tasking is the skill that actually produces good work.
